items.title: William Russell Interview, 1975-02-02
items.q: When I talked to Johnny Dodds—we were writing Jazzmen in those days, 1938—and I was asking about the breakup of the Oliver Band.

ctx.x: Well, you could tell me how American music got started. It started at the beginning.

So anyway, to get back to the point, Gene Williams had heard these records and agreed with me too that at least Bunk showed some possibilities. You couldn't really tell much how he played, both because his lip wasn't in shape and just by himself. The type of trumpet playing that Bunk did, which was a remarkable thing, and yet by itself it wouldn't sound that effective. Bunk was hardly ever on the beat, so if you didn't hear him patting his foot and all there, you could really tell of course where the beat is, but…

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-08-31
items.q: Before that I'd gone to see people like Jimmy Noon, Johnny Dodds, and Armstrong, and met a few of my favorite New Orleans musicians.

ctx.x: You want to talk about some of these musicians you've encountered in the course of your career now?

Yes, I might talk a little bit. I happened to pick up an old big box at home I have called Notes, and I dug out a few of the notebooks and other things. One package of notes envelope called Jazzmen material that we collected in 1938 when we were working on Jazzmen. Unfortunately then, we not only didn't have tape recording, we didn't have any other recorders. Nobody was hardly recording interviews.
